people.name: Muhammad

chapters.title: The beginning of revelation
chapters.text: Islamic tradition describes Muhammad receiving revelation at Hira and returning to Khadijah, who reassures him. The report is transmitted by Aisha in Sahih al-Bukhari.

chapters.title: A community in Medina
chapters.text: The migration to Medina in 622 marks a central turning point in his mission. Muhammad died in 632. The Qur’an calls him the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets.

sources.note: Sahih collection in Sunni tradition; this is a transmitted report, not a contemporary eyewitness document.

people.name: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid

chapters.title: A return from Hira
chapters.text: In the report of the first revelation, Muhammad returns frightened to his wife Khadijah. She reassures him by recalling his care for relatives, guests, and people in need.

chapters.title: Seeking understanding
chapters.text: The same report says Khadijah takes Muhammad to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal to hear what happened. Her response forms a central part of the transmitted account of revelation’s beginning.

sources.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3
sources.note: Sahih collection in Sunni tradition; this is a transmitted report, not a contemporary eyewitness document.

people.uncertainty: Her exact birth year and age at marriage are not asserted. This account follows the Sunni hadith report.

people.name: Aisha bint Abi Bakr

chapters.title: Preserving an account
chapters.text: Aisha is the named transmitter of the account of the beginning of revelation in Sahih al-Bukhari. Her narration preserves the story of Muhammad’s return to Khadijah.

chapters.title: A source of understanding
chapters.text: A report from Abu Musa describes the Companions consulting Aisha when they needed help understanding a hadith. It bears witness to her place in the transmission of religious knowledge.

sources.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3

people.name: Abu Bakr

chapters.title: Companionship
chapters.text: Abu Bakr was an early Muslim and accompanied Muhammad on the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622.

chapters.title: After 632
chapters.text: He became the first caliph after Muhammad’s death and ruled until 634. His reign included the Ridda wars and the consolidation of rule in Arabia.

people.uncertainty: Succession and religious authority are interpreted differently in Sunni and Shia traditions. A short historical summary does not settle those differences.

people.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab

chapters.title: A succession
chapters.text: Umar succeeded Abu Bakr in 634 and led the caliphate until 644.

chapters.title: A changing state
chapters.text: His reign saw expansion into Byzantine and Sasanian territories and changes to the administration of the growing state.

sources.title: Umar ibn al-Khattab — World History Encyclopedia

people.uncertainty: Succession and religious authority are interpreted differently in Sunni and Shia traditions. A short historical summary does not settle those differences.

people.name: Uthman ibn Affan

chapters.title: Leadership
chapters.text: Uthman succeeded Umar and ruled from 644 to 656. His death came during a rebellion against his government.

chapters.title: The written Qur’an
chapters.text: Sahih al-Bukhari reports Uthman commissioning copies of the Qur’an from manuscripts held by Hafsah and sending copies to different regions.

sources.title: Uthman ibn Affan — World History Encyclopedia

people.name: Ali ibn Abi Talib

chapters.title: Family and community
chapters.text: Ali was Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law. He became caliph in 656.

chapters.title: A divided community
chapters.text: His caliphate unfolded during the first civil war. He was assassinated in 661. Sunni tradition counts him as the fourth rightly guided caliph; Shia tradition recognises him as the first imam.

sources.title: Ali ibn Abi Talib — World History Encyclopedia

people.uncertainty: Succession and religious authority are interpreted differently in Sunni and Shia traditions. A short historical summary does not settle those differences.

people.name: Al-Khwarizmi

chapters.title: Working in Baghdad
chapters.text: Al-Khwarizmi worked under the patronage of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma’mun. His mathematical writing addressed practical problems as well as methods of calculation.

chapters.title: Words that travelled
chapters.text: His algebra treatise helped give algebra its name. The word algorithm derives from the Latin form of his name; his work helped transmit Indian numeral methods.

people.uncertainty: His birthplace is uncertain and his life dates approximate. He did not invent the Indian numerals.

people.name: Ibn al-Haytham

chapters.title: A life in inquiry
chapters.text: Ibn al-Haytham wrote on mathematics, astronomy, and optics. His career connected Basra with Egypt.

chapters.title: Light and vision
chapters.text: His Book of Optics examined vision, reflection, and refraction. He argued that light enters the eye from objects, and used experiments in investigating optical questions.

people.uncertainty: Accounts of his dealings with al-Hakim differ. Stories of feigned madness are not presented here as settled facts. Death dates vary around 1039–1040.

people.name: Al-Biruni

chapters.title: Observation and calculation
chapters.text: Born near Kath in Khwarazm, al-Biruni studied astronomy and mathematics. His observations helped determine geographical positions.

chapters.title: Studying India
chapters.text: He studied Sanskrit sources and wrote about Indian religion, customs, astronomy, and learning. His work emerged amid political upheaval and Ghaznavid expansion.

people.uncertainty: Dates of particular journeys are uncertain. This summary does not claim his travel was voluntary.

people.name: Ibn Sina
people.date: c. 970 or 980–1037 CE · birth year disputed
people.place: Afshana near Bukhara; later Hamadan and Isfahan

chapters.title: Learning and movement
chapters.text: Ibn Sina grew up in the intellectual world of Bukhara. His career later took him to several courts, where he worked as a physician and adviser.

chapters.title: An enduring body of work
chapters.text: His Canon of Medicine became influential in medical teaching, including through Latin translation. His philosophical writings shaped debate across the Islamic world. He died in Hamadan in 1037.

sources.title: Ibn Sina — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

people.uncertainty: The birth-year estimates are displayed as alternatives, not an exact date or a continuous confidence interval. Bukhara is an approximate regional locator. The principal biographical source is his autobiography with al-Juzjani’s continuation, discussed in the linked scholarship.

dateEvidence.text: 980 is the conventional birth year. The consulted Stanford biography argues for approximately 970. His death in Hamadan is dated to 1037.

placeEvidence.text: His autobiography, continued by al-Juzjani, places his birth in Afshana near Bukhara. The map locates the Bukhara region; it does not mark an exact birth house.

people.name: Salah al-Din

chapters.title: Power and alliances
chapters.text: Salah al-Din, known as Saladin, built his power in Egypt and Syria through both military action and diplomacy.

chapters.title: Jerusalem in 1187
chapters.text: His forces defeated the Crusader army at Hattin and captured Jerusalem in 1187. His career also involved wars against Muslim rivals; it cannot be reduced to later stories of chivalry.

people.uncertainty: Birth dates are given as 1137 or 1138 in different references. Later heroic literature is not treated as direct evidence.

people.name: Mansa Musa
people.place: Mali and the pilgrimage to Mecca

chapters.title: A West African ruler
chapters.text: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire. His pilgrimage brought him through Cairo in 1324, where accounts of his wealth attracted attention.

chapters.title: Learning and exchange
chapters.text: His patronage supported Islamic buildings and scholarship. His life belongs to a wider history of trans-Saharan trade, pilgrimage, and intellectual exchange.

people.uncertainty: The end of his reign is disputed. Modern dollar valuations and “richest person ever” rankings are not reliable historical measurements.

people.name: Ibn Battuta

chapters.title: Leaving home
chapters.text: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 to undertake the pilgrimage to Mecca. His travels continued far beyond the initial pilgrimage.

chapters.title: Remembering the journey
chapters.text: His recollections became the Rihla, dictated after his return. It is an important account of connected Muslim societies, but a travel narrative requires critical reading rather than treating every passage as an independently confirmed visit.

sources.title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta — UC Berkeley ORIAS

people.uncertainty: Dates and routes in the Rihla are debated. The map marks Tangier, his point of departure, not every claimed destination.

people.name: Mimar Sinan

chapters.title: Building for a city
chapters.text: Sinan designed the Selimiye Mosque complex in Edirne for Selim II. Its great dome and four minarets remain defining features of the city’s skyline.

chapters.title: Beyond a prayer hall
chapters.text: The complex included educational and commercial spaces alongside the mosque. It illustrates the Ottoman külliye: a group of buildings serving religious and social functions together.

sources.title: Selimiye Mosque and its Social Complex — UNESCO

people.uncertainty: This entry focuses on a surviving, documented work rather than reconstructing uncertain details of his early life.

people.name: Ahmed Zewail

chapters.title: A new timescale
chapters.text: Ahmed Zewail’s research made it possible to study atomic motion during chemical reactions on femtosecond timescales. This work helped establish femtochemistry.

chapters.title: Science in a connected world
chapters.text: A Caltech professor, he received the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His later work included four-dimensional electron microscopy. He died in 2016.

people.uncertainty: Included in the modern history of people from the Muslim world; scientific achievement is not used as evidence for a theological claim.

people.name: Zayd ibn Harithah

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an explicitly names Zayd in the passage concerning the end of his marriage and the Prophet’s subsequent marriage.

sources.title: Qur’an 33:37
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The verse itself names Zayd; the full identification is supplied by the tafsir shown with the verse. The Qur’an does not name his former wife in this passage.

people.name: Abu Lahab

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Surah al-Masad names Abu Lahab and declares that his wealth and gains will not benefit him. The chapter also refers to his wife.

sources.title: Qur’an 111:1-5
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: This is the Qur’anic account. The chapter does not supply his full genealogy or life dates.

people.name: Imran

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an identifies the woman making a vow concerning her unborn child as the wife of Imran.

sources.title: Qur’an 3:35
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: This passage gives no detailed biography of Imran. He is not identified here with other historical people who share the name.

people.name: The wife of Imran

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The wife of Imran dedicates what is in her womb to divine service and asks Allah to accept her offering.

sources.title: Qur’an 3:35
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Her personal name is not stated in this verse. Later names should be attributed to their own sources, not presented as Qur’anic wording.

people.name: Azar

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Ibrahim addresses Azar in a passage challenging the taking of idols as gods. The Arabic text uses the kinship term ab.

sources.title: Qur’an 6:74
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Translations commonly render the relationship as father. Some exegetical traditions interpret the relationship differently; this entry does not settle that debate.

people.name: Luqman

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an describes Luqman as receiving wisdom and being told to show gratitude to Allah. His counsel to his son warns against associating partners with Allah.

sources.title: Qur’an 31:12-13
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: His name is explicit, but these verses do not give a birth date, ethnicity, or profession. Those details are not invented.

people.name: Uzayr
people.role: A name in a theological passage

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Uzayr is named in a Qur’anic passage rejecting claims of divine sonship.

sources.title: Qur’an 9:30
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The verse is a theological statement, not a full biography or a description of what all Jewish people in every period believe. His prophetic status is not asserted here.

people.name: Talut

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: An unnamed prophet tells his people that Allah has appointed Talut as king. Objections about wealth are answered with reference to his knowledge and stature.

sources.title: Qur’an 2:247
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Talut is commonly rendered Saul in translation. No precise date is supplied by the verse.

people.name: Jalut

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an recounts the defeat of an opposing force and states that Dawud killed Jalut. It then describes Dawud receiving kingship and wisdom.

sources.title: Qur’an 2:251
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Commonly rendered Goliath in translation. Later descriptions of his appearance are not added to this entry.

people.name: Qarun

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Qarun is described as belonging to Musa’s people and acting arrogantly toward them. The passage describes his enormous stores of wealth and the counsel given to him.

sources.title: Qur’an 28:76
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The Qur’anic account is not assigned a historical financial valuation or an independently verified date.

people.name: Haman

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Pharaoh addresses Haman and orders construction of a high structure while making a claim about the God of Musa.

sources.title: Qur’an 28:38
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The Haman of this account is not automatically identified with a similarly named person in another text.

people.name: Pharaoh in Musa’s account

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an presents Pharaoh making a claim of exclusive divinity to his chiefs and directing Haman to build a high structure.

sources.title: Qur’an 28:38
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Pharaoh is a title. Identification with a particular Egyptian ruler is not established by this verse.

people.name: Al-Samiri

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: In Surah Taha, Musa is told that his people have been tested in his absence and that al-Samiri has led them astray.

sources.title: Qur’an 20:85
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: This designation does not establish his full personal name or a modern ethnic identity.

people.name: The Queen of Sheba

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: In the account of Sulayman, the hoopoe reports finding a woman ruling over a people, supplied with many things and possessing a great throne.

sources.title: Qur’an 27:23
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The Qur’an does not give her personal name. Bilqis belongs to later tradition; it is not substituted for the Qur’an’s unnamed identification.

people.name: The wife of Pharaoh

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an presents Pharaoh’s wife as an example for believers. She asks Allah for a home near Him in Paradise and for rescue from Pharaoh and wrongdoing.

sources.title: Qur’an 66:11
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: Her personal name is not stated in the verse. Asiyah is a name found in hadith and later tradition and requires separate attribution.

people.name: The sister of Musa

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: Musa’s mother tells his sister to follow him. The account describes her watching him from a distance without the others noticing.

sources.title: Qur’an 28:11
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The Qur’an does not state her personal name. This entry does not import a name from another tradition.

people.name: The wife of Nuh

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The Qur’an names the wife of Nuh by her relationship in an example of disbelief. Her relationship to a righteous servant does not protect her from judgement.

sources.title: Qur’an 66:10
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The verse does not give her personal name. Its language of betrayal is not expanded into an invented allegation of sexual infidelity.

people.name: The wife of Lut

chapters.title: In the source
chapters.text: The wife of Lut appears with the wife of Nuh in the Qur’an’s example of people whose family relationships did not protect them from judgement.

sources.title: Qur’an 66:10
sources.note: Verse reference; story text is an original paraphrase, not a translation.

people.uncertainty: The verse does not give her personal name. Her entry remains distinct from the wife of Nuh.
